section_summary: This section completes a comprehensive 1934 consular report on Japanese migration, including government-assisted emigration to Brazil and Manchuria, immigration into Japan, internal colonial settlement, restrictive legislation, and extensive statistical appendices. It then contains reports and correspondence concerning the treatment of foreign entertainers and other temporary workers in Japan. The final group examines the administrative exclusion of alien laborers—especially Chinese—and restrictions on alien landownership, with translations of the principal 1899 ordinances and related correspondence with Yale historian Samuel F. Bemis.

subfiles.title: Trend of Migratory Movements—Japan
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul, American Consulate General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: A comprehensive study of Japanese overseas emigration, immigration into Japan, colonial settlement, and migration restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the government-directed character of Japanese emigration, especially assisted settlement in Brazil, and assesses new restrictions in Brazil, Peru, and the Philippines. It reviews disappointing colonization efforts in Manchuria, Hokkaido, Sakhalin, Korea, Taiwan, and the South Seas Mandate, while noting substantial Korean immigration into Japan. It concludes that emigration makes little contribution to relieving population pressure and includes sources and statistical tables on overseas populations, permits, occupations, and ages.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs summary of the Japanese migration report
subfiles.about: An internal précis of the Tokyo report on Japanese migration.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights the distribution of Japanese abroad, the government-controlled nature of emigration, and the negligible annual net outflow from Japan. It emphasizes failed subsidized settlement in Manchuria, the scale of Korean immigration into Japan, and the limited success of migration to Japanese-controlled territories.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and rating of “Trend of Migratory Movements—Japan”
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, signed for the Secretary by Wilbur J. Carr
subfiles.to: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the migration report and rates it excellent.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges receipt of the Consulate General’s October 19 report prepared by J. M. Allison. It assigns the report a rating of “Excellent” and directs that Allison be informed.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs summary of Report No. 145
subfiles.about: A summary of the Tokyo report on temporary admission of foreign performers.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Japanese law does not expressly discriminate against foreign actors and musicians but that police treat them arbitrarily and usually limit their stays. It contrasts this with generous American treatment of Japanese theatrical organizations and finds legitimate grounds for complaint.

subfiles.title: Conditions of Temporary Admission and Residence of Instrumental Musicians, Other Musicians, Actors, Artists, and Choristers
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.about: The report explains Japanese admission law and police practice toward foreign performers.
subfiles.summary: Foreign performers were governed by general non-immigrant rules rather than special legislation, but police frequently demanded local guarantees, enforced short transit visas, or alleged threats to public order. The experience of D. Kaili, Mrs. Kaili, and Pearl Alama illustrates how valid visas and successive employment guarantees did not prevent expulsion. Allison concludes that inconsistent and arbitrary administration, rather than the general legal principle, caused dissatisfaction.

subfiles.title: Conditions of Temporary Admission and Residence of Aliens for Employment Other Than Specified in Report No. 145
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.about: A short report stating that no special rules governed temporary alien workers outside the performer categories.
subfiles.summary: Allison reports that temporary alien employment outside the categories covered by Report No. 145 was subject to the general admission and residence rules. He refers the Department to Hutchinson’s November 19, 1932 report and states that the regulations had not changed.

subfiles.title: Nagasaki response concerning special immigration reports
subfiles.from: Glen Bruner, American Vice Consul, Nagasaki
subfiles.about: Nagasaki advises that Tokyo will prepare the requested national immigration reports.
subfiles.summary: Bruner refers to the Department’s September 14 instruction. Because the requested reports are national in scope, the Consulate General at Tokyo will prepare them.

subfiles.title: Kobe response concerning special immigration reports
subfiles.about: Kobe states that no separate local report will be prepared because Tokyo is consolidating the response.
subfiles.summary: Donovan reports that the Consulate General at Tokyo intends to prepare a consolidated report for Japan. Kobe therefore will not submit a separate report.

subfiles.title: Nagoya response concerning special immigration reports
subfiles.from: Joseph E. Newton, American Vice Consul, Nagoya
subfiles.about: Nagoya defers the nationally scoped immigration reports to the Tokyo Consulate General.
subfiles.summary: Newton acknowledges the Department’s instruction requesting special immigration reports. He states that the Tokyo Consulate General will prepare them because they concern national policy.

subfiles.title: Yokohama response concerning special immigration reports
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Yokohama confirms that Tokyo will report on temporary admission of performers and other alien workers.
subfiles.summary: Boyce repeats the two subjects requested by the Department: admission of performers and admission of other aliens for employment. He states that the Consulate General at Tokyo will provide the national reports.

subfiles.title: Taihoku response concerning special immigration reports
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Taihoku reports that its district information has been sent to Tokyo for inclusion in a national report.
subfiles.summary: McConaughy acknowledges the Department’s circular instruction. In accordance with directions from the Consul General, the Taihoku office forwarded its information to Tokyo rather than producing a separate report.

subfiles.title: Request for information on Japanese immigration and alien landownership laws
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Hornbeck requests current information for a Yale professor on Japanese restrictions affecting alien immigration and landownership.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck asks how Japanese immigration and land laws operate in practice, particularly against Chinese laborers and farmers in Japan and Korea. He cites earlier Embassy reports and asks Grew to distinguish communicable information from confidential material. A prompt, concise response is preferred to a delayed polished study.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Ambassador Grew’s reply to Samuel F. Bemis
subfiles.about: Hornbeck sends Bemis a confidential copy of Grew’s response on Japanese immigration and alien land laws.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains that he requested the information after Bemis’s December visit and has now received Grew’s reply. Bemis may use the substance at his discretion but must omit confidential passages and avoid attribution to an official source; the enclosure is to be returned.

subfiles.title: Current enforcement of Japanese immigration and alien landownership laws
subfiles.doc_type: embassy letter and informal legal report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grew reports on the practical exclusion of alien laborers and administrative obstacles to Chinese landownership.
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that broadly worded ordinances delegate extensive, unappealable authority to local police, allowing Japan to exclude unwanted aliens without overtly discriminatory statutes. Chinese may enter without passports or visas under a reciprocal arrangement if they possess “show money,” but they lack special occupational rights and laborers remain excludable. Although the reciprocal prohibition in the 1925 Alien Land Ownership Law had not formally been activated, administrative opposition and potential deportation effectively deterred Chinese farmers from acquiring land in Japan or Korea.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 352
subfiles.to: Japanese administrative authorities and the public
subfiles.about: The ordinance regulates residence and employment outside former foreign settlements by aliens lacking treaty-based freedom of residence.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance permits qualifying aliens to reside and trade outside former settlements but excludes alien laborers unless they receive special administrative permission. It authorizes the Home Minister to define laborers and enforcement rules, provides a fine for violations, and sets August 4, 1899 as the effective date.

subfiles.title: Home Department Ordinance No. 421
subfiles.to: Prefectural governors and the governor of Hokkaido
subfiles.about: The ordinance supplies enforcement rules and defines the alien laborers covered by Imperial Ordinance No. 352.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance designates prefectural governors and the governor of Hokkaido as the competent administrative officials. It defines covered labor as agriculture, fishing, mining, engineering, construction, manufacturing, transportation, and miscellaneous work, while exempting domestic service. Officials may revoke permits when they deem revocation necessary for public welfare.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of confidential immigration and land-tenure information
subfiles.about: Bemis acknowledges receipt of Hornbeck’s letter and confidential enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Bemis thanks Hornbeck for the January 31 letter and the explanation of Japanese administration of immigration and land tenure. He assures Hornbeck that he will handle the information under the stated restrictions.

subfiles.title: Return of confidential enclosure
subfiles.about: Bemis returns the enclosure previously discussed with Hornbeck.
subfiles.summary: Bemis sends back the enclosure that Hornbeck had mentioned during a recent conversation at the Cosmos Club. The brief note closes the exchange over the confidential material.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Grew’s report on Japanese immigration and alien landownership
subfiles.doc_type: embassy letter copy, incomplete in this section
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: A duplicate copy restates Grew’s findings on alien exclusion, Chinese entry privileges, and alien landownership.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats the explanation that local authorities exercise broad, unappealable discretion under general immigration ordinances and can exclude alien workers without facially discriminatory legislation. It describes the passport exemption and “show money” arrangement for Chinese entrants, while noting that Chinese laborers still face occupational restrictions. It also explains the dormant reciprocal provision of the Alien Land Ownership Law and the practical obstacles facing Chinese agricultural purchasers; the duplicate continues beyond page 152.
